content:
One widely circulated critique says that Muhammad (peace be upon him) predicted the end of the world 500 years after his call, which gives the year 1110 CE. The date passed, so the critique concludes that he was a false prophet.

The claim rests on reports about "half a day". Five points follow: what the report says, what the Quran says about the Hour, what the wording allows, how a day is measured, and how the Prophet and the scholars handled the question. Where a report's wording could not be confirmed, the article says so.

The critique is worth answering because it has a clear test. If the Prophet set a date and the date passed, the charge is serious, since the Quran itself says that a prophet who invents a statement about God would be judged severely (69:44–46). The answer therefore has to show what the report says, who added the number, and how the earliest readers understood it.

The claim in its strongest form runs as follows. Abu Dawud records a saying in which the Prophet hoped that his community would be given a delay of half a day before its Lord. When Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, the narrator, was asked how long half a day was, he answered that it was 500 years.[1] Counting from the first revelation in about 610 CE gives 1110 CE, a date that passed long ago.

Part of this is sound. The report exists, it sits in a major collection, al-Albani grades it sound, and the figure 500 is in the report. The figure, though, is the explanation given by Sa'd, the Companion who narrated it; the Prophet's words in the report do not state it. The critique's route through "a day is 1,000 years" is a detour either way. The critique also cites al-Tabari, and on this point it is right. In his History, al-Tabari reads the half-day report as a statement of how much time remained: five hundred years, half of a divine day of a thousand. Joining it to a saying of Ibn Abbas that the world lasts seven thousand years, he concludes that about 6,500 years had passed by the time the Prophet spoke.[2] A major classical scholar therefore did read the report as a span of time. His conclusion rests on his own arithmetic, built from the Companion's gloss and a separate report, and the entries that follow examine whether the report itself requires it. Whether this is the Prophet's most often repeated prophecy cannot be confirmed.

Several passages say that the time of the Hour belongs to God alone. Quran 7:187 says that knowledge of it is with the Lord, that none can reveal its time but Him, and that it comes suddenly. Quran 33:63 gives the same answer to people who ask, and adds that the Hour may well be near. Quran 31:34 lists it among the matters that only God knows.[3]

Quran 79:42-44 describes the questioners asking when it will arrive, and the reply is that its final term is with the Lord.[4] A critic can fairly point to 33:63 as a statement of nearness. It is a statement of nearness with no year attached, and the same verse tells the Prophet to say that the knowledge is with God. A date would contradict all of these verses, so a report that sounds like a date has to be read in a way that fits them.

The Prophet also listed events that must happen before the Hour, among them the ten major signs and many lesser ones, several of which had not occurred in his lifetime or in the centuries after.[5] A man who gave his followers a list of signs still to come was not, on the face of it, telling them that the end would arrive on a fixed date within a few centuries. The reports about the signs and the half-day report have to be read together, and together they describe a future of uncertain length.

As reported, the Prophet says "I hope" (arjū). He does not say that the world will end. What he hopes for is that his community will not fall short of being given half a day, which means that it will last at least that long.[6] A floor is not a deadline. The community has lasted far more than 500 years, so the hoped-for minimum was met and nothing in the report failed.

A critic may answer that the saying still implies that the end might come soon after the half day. Nothing in the wording states that. The report also gives no starting point. Counting from the call gives 1110 CE; counting from the migration to Medina in 622 CE gives 1122 CE; counting from his birth gives another year. The choice of 610 CE is the critique's own.

There is also the question of tone. The report presents the Prophet hoping for his community and asking for more time for it, which is how the narrator and the early readers understood it. A countdown is a different kind of statement, and the critique has to read a hope as a forecast to find one.

The critique's own arithmetic depends on Quran 22:47, which says that a day with the Lord is like a thousand years of human counting. Quran 32:5 uses a similar figure for the affairs that rise to Him. Quran 70:4 speaks of a day whose measure is fifty thousand years.[7] The Quran therefore uses more than one measure, and none of these verses is a conversion table for the Hour.

Half of 1,000 is 500, so a reader can link the report to 22:47, and some have. The exchange itself gives only a number and does not cite the verse; the link is an inference by readers. It is a reasonable inference, and also an optional one. The report holds up without it, since the number 500 is already there and the question is only what the number means.

The Quran's own use of the image of a thousand years points away from calculation. Quran 22:47 comes in answer to people who mocked the Prophet by asking him to hurry the punishment he warned of. The reply is that God does not break His promise, and that a day with Him is like a thousand years of their counting. The verse rebukes impatience with God's timing, and it does not supply a unit for working out the end.

In the well-known hadith of Gabriel, the Prophet was asked about the Hour and replied: "One who is asked knows no more than the one who is inquiring."[8] That is a direct statement of the limit of his own knowledge. Other reports have him joining two fingers and saying that he and the Hour were sent like these two, which speaks of closeness in the order of history and gives no date.[9]

The later scholars did not conclude that the passing of 500 years refuted him. Writing in the ninth century of the Hijra, al-Suyuti argued in a short treatise that the community would outlast a thousand years, though not by as much as five hundred more, reasoning from reports that set the world's span at about seven thousand years.[10] Other scholars rejected his calculation, on the ground that the reports he used are very weak and that only God knows the Hour. Al-Tabari's reading did imply an end some five centuries after the Prophet, so the critique has a classical precedent. Other scholars rejected such calculations, on the ground that only God knows the Hour, and the Quran and the hadith of Gabriel stand with them.

Expectations of this kind appeared at other moments in Muslim history. As the year 1000 of the Hijra approached, some Muslims in India and elsewhere expected the world to end or a new age to begin, and the Mughal emperor Akbar commissioned a history of the first Islamic millennium.[11] Al-Suyuti's treatise was written partly to answer such fears. The year passed, and the scholars who had warned against setting dates were vindicated again.

Other traditions have faced the same problem. Christians have debated for centuries what Jesus meant when he said that some of those standing with him would not taste death before seeing the kingdom of God come, and in 1844 the followers of William Miller, who had calculated the date of the second coming, lived through what they called the Great Disappointment.[12] The temptation to put a date on the end is human and widespread. The Quran's refusal to name one is the clearest answer to it.

The bottom line

The report behind the claim is real, and it does contain the number 500. It is a hope that the community would last at least half a day, it names no starting point, and the Quran and the hadith of Gabriel both place the time of the Hour with God alone. A minimum that is exceeded is not a failed prediction.

A critic can fairly point out that al-Tabari read the report as a countdown. The answer is that his reading was one scholar's calculation, that the Prophet's own words give no figure, and that the Quran places the time of the Hour with God alone.

A reader weighing the critique should therefore separate three things: the Prophet's words, which express a hope and give no figure; the Companion's explanation, which supplies the number; and the later calculations, which some scholars made and others rejected. Only the first carries the Prophet's authority, and it promised nothing that failed.

Notes

  1. Sunan Abi Dawud 4350 (Book of Battles, chapter on the onset of the Hour), from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas; graded sound by al-Albani.
  2. Al-Tabari, The History of al-Tabari, vol. 1, General Introduction and From the Creation to the Flood, trans. Franz Rosenthal (Albany: SUNY Press, 1989), pp. 182–183, "The Duration of the World".
  3. Quran 7:187; 33:63; 31:34.
  4. Quran 79:42-44.
  5. Sahih Muslim 2901, Book of Tribulations and Signs of the Hour, report of Hudhayfa ibn Asid.
  6. Sunan Abi Dawud 4350, ibid.
  7. Quran 22:47; 32:5; 70:4.
  8. Sahih Muslim 8a (Book of Faith), the hadith of Gabriel.
  9. Sahih al-Bukhari 6504 (Book of Softening the Hearts), from Anas: "I have been sent, and the Hour, as these two.". Checked on sunnah.com (chapter "I have been sent, and the Hour as these two", report of Anas ibn Malik); Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani, Fath al-Bari (Salafiyya edition), vol. 11, p. 347 (Shamela text).
  10. Al-Suyuti, al-Kashf an Mujawazat Hadhihi al-Umma al-Alf; on his conclusion and its rejection by other scholars, Darul Iftaa Askimam, "The life of my community will not exceed 1500 years: true or fake?", islamqa.org, answer 126387.
  11. On the Tarikh-i Alfi and millennial expectations at the Mughal court, see A. Azfar Moin, The Millennial Sovereign: Sacred Kingship and Sainthood in Islam (New York: Columbia University Press, 2012).
  12. Mark 9:1; on the Millerite movement and the "Great Disappointment" of 22 October 1844, see Ronald L. Numbers and Jonathan M. Butler, eds., The Disappointed: Millerism and Millenarianism in the Nineteenth Century (Bloomington: Indiana University Press, 1987).
